title: developer-sandbox-benchmarking-playbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary
This playbook describes the developer-local runtime sandbox and associated benchmarking + profiling workflows used to reproduce key production behaviors without requiring full cluster access. The sandbox is intentionally lightweight and deterministic: it models the runtime dispatch, a KV cache shim, a kernel-proxy for scheduling experiments, and easy-to-run microbenchmarks. Use this guide to iterate on kernel scheduler patches, evaluate batching strategies, and validate optimization hypotheses before graduating changes to the full perf suite.

Scope
- Reproduce request lifecycle: API -> dispatcher -> kernel-proxy -> model executor (mock or quantized engine).
- Run microbenchmarks that mimic production prompt shapes (short, medium, long) and multi-turn chat traces.
- Exercise scheduling policies (fair-share, priority-driven, cooperative preemption) in a reproducible environment.
- Capture perf traces (CPU/GPU timelines), kernel occupancy, and per-token cost estimates.
- Limitations: does not emulate multi-tenant noisy neighbors at scale, and GPU topology is single-node only. See Known Differences section.

Prerequisites
1) Linux workstation with Docker 20.10+ or a macOS machine with Docker Desktop and a supported GPU passthrough (optional).
2) tools/runtime-sandbox repo checked out (internal): git clone git@repo.internal:redwood/tools/runtime-sandbox.git
3) Python 3.10+, pipenv or virtualenv for running harness scripts.

Sandbox Components (what runs locally)
- runtime-dispatcher-lite: lightweight HTTP front-end that accepts Redwood API-style requests and translates compute work into a scheduling request.
- kvcached-shim: in-memory KV cache with controllable hit-rate to simulate warm/cold sessions.
- kernel-proxy: process that implements a subset of production kernel selection + queuing logic; pluggable policies: simple_fifo, fair_share, priority_shepherd.
- model-mock: tunable latency stub or a real local quantized engine (GGML/onnxruntime path) for end-to-end verification.

Quickstart: run the sandbox (example)
1) Start the sandbox (default ports: 8080 dispatcher, 9090 proxy):
```bash
cd tools/runtime-sandbox
./scripts/start_sandbox.sh --workers 4 --policy priority_shepherd --kv-hit-rate 0.2
```
2) Run a short prompt microbenchmark (50 token generation, batch size 8):
```bash
./benchmarks/run_local_microbench.py --endpoint http://localhost:8080/generate --prompt-file examples/short_prompts.txt --batch-size 8 --tokens 50 --samples 100
```
3) Collect traces and open local report:
```bash
./scripts/collect_traces.sh --out=artifacts/run-$(date +%s)
open artifacts/run-*/index.html  # (Linux: xdg-open)
```

Benchmark Catalog (recommended microbenchmarks)
- short_prompt_50: 50 tokens, mean prompt length 12 tokens, simulates chat replies and low-latency assistant responses.
- medium_prompt_200: 200 tokens, mean prompt length 80 tokens, represents longer instruction completions.
- long_prompt_1024: 1024 tokens, stress test for KV cache and kernel memory usage.
- multi_turn_continuation: sequence of 4 calls with KV cache warmup between calls.
- mixed_priority_mixture: concurrent clients with priority labels (gold/silver/free) to exercise preemption.

Example benchmark command (mixed workload)
```bash
./benchmarks/run_local_mixed.sh \
  --clients 40 --gold-share 0.1 --silver-share 0.3 --policy fair_share \
  --duration 300 --output artifacts/mixed-$(date +%s).json
```

Kernel Scheduling Experiments
We expose the following knobs in kernel-proxy to emulate production scheduling behavior:
- batch_window_ms: how long to wait to form a batch before dispatch. Typical test values: 1, 4, 8, 16 ms.
- max_batch_tokens: maximum token budget allowed for a single batch.
- preempt_granularity: slice size used for cooperative preemption (in tokens).
- priority_weight: mapping table for gold/silver/free request weight.

Experiment template (compare batch_window_ms)
1) Start sandbox with identical worker count and model-mock latency profile.
2) Run short_prompt_50 with batch_window_ms set to 1, 4, 8, 16. Each run: 3 warmup minutes + 10 minute sampling.
3) Metrics to record: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), mean batch size, dispatch queue depth.
4) Success criteria: for short_prompt_50, p95 <= 120ms and throughput drop <= 5% relative to baseline.

Profiling and Tracing Guidance
- Enable kernel telemetry: set env RUNTIME_TELEMETRY=1 in start_sandbox.sh to capture per-kernel timings and memory high-water marks.
- GPU traces: when running with a local GPU engine, enable CUPTI tracing via ./scripts/start_gpu_tracing.sh. For CPU-only runs, use perf and flamegraphs.
- Annotate traces with request provenance: the dispatcher attaches request_id and priority_tag to every scheduling event. Include these when uploading traces to the central trace collector.

Trace artifact format and required fields
When you upload a trace for triage, include the following in the artifact zip:
- run_metadata.json (fields: run_id, start_ts, policy, worker_count, kv_hit_rate, model_path)
- kernel_timings.csv (columns: timestamp, kernel_name, duration_ms, occupancy_pct, allocated_bytes)
- batch_events.ndjson (one line per batch event: request_ids[], batch_size, policy, outcome)
- system_monitor.log (CPU, GPU, memory samples at 1s resolution)

Example run_metadata.json (literal snippet)
```json
{
  "run_id": "local-20260210-001",
  "policy": "priority_shepherd",
  "worker_count": 4,
  "kv_hit_rate": 0.2,
  "model_path": "local-ggml/7b-q4_0.bin"
}
```

Runbook: triage workflow for an unexpected latency regression
1) Reproduce locally using the same artifact and policy. If you cannot reproduce, escalate to runtime-sre with full artifact.
2) Run `./benchmarks/run_local_microbench.py` with `--diagnostic=true` to produce kernel_timings and batch_events.
3) Check batch size distribution and batch wait times. If mean batch_size drops by >25% vs baseline, suspect batching regressions.
4) Inspect kernel_timings.csv for spikes in a specific kernel. If a single kernel shows >50% increase in median duration, flag as kernel regression and attach minimal repro to a kernel-owner PR.
5) If GPU memory HWM increased significantly, run the memory-fragmentation diagnostic script: `./scripts/gpu_memory_frag_diag.sh`.
6) Document findings in the triage template and update the related run in the benchmarking dashboard.

Known Differences vs Production
- Multi-node routing and remote shard topology are not modeled; cross-node latencies and NUMA effects may be missing.
- The sandbox runs a single GPU device; device-local scheduling differences and inter-GPU NVLink behaviors are not captured.
- Autoscaling and burst capacity behavior is not exercised.
- Real tenant-induced KV-cache conflicts are out of scope.

Best Practices for Developers
- Start with model-mock for rapid iterations; only switch to a local quantized engine (GGML/ONNX) when validating memory and kernel changes.
- Keep run_metadata for every experiment. It is the single source of truth when comparing runs.
- Use stable random seeds when benchmarking (pass --seed <n>) to reduce variance.
- Run at least 3 independent samples for each configuration and report median with IQR.

Onboarding Checklist (for new runtime contributors)
1) Read this playbook and the runtime profiling guidelines page.
2) Run the short_prompt_50 microbenchmark and verify baseline numbers (p95 <= 120ms on a dev workstation with model-mock).
3) Submit one small change (e.g., tweak batch_window_ms) and show the before/after artifacts in a PR.
4) Request review from kernel owners and runtime-sre for approval.

Troubleshooting common errors
- `Connection refused` on kernel-proxy: ensure the proxy is up (docker ps) and ports 9090/9091 are free.
- `Empty batches` warnings: check dispatcher logs; increase batch_window_ms by 2ms for noise-sensitive environments.
- `OOM on model-mock`: reduce model size or run with --simulated-memory=true flag.

Appendix: example minimal policy YAML for kernel-proxy
```yaml
policy: priority_shepherd
params:
  batch_window_ms: 4
  max_batch_tokens: 2048
  preempt_granularity: 32
  priority_weight:
    gold: 3
    silver: 2
    free: 1
```

If you have questions about extending the sandbox or integrating additional telemetry hooks, reach out to the runtime-observability channel on Slack and attach run artifacts.
